newsitem.title: UK: Dlr struggles in Europe, soft US data sparks drop.
newsitem.headline: Dlr struggles in Europe, soft US data sparks drop.

text.p: The dollar was struggling near its session lows against the mark and yen in late European trade, battling against dollar sales sparked by slightly weaker-than-expected U.S. jobs data for June.
The dollar showed a surprisingly sharp reaction to the data considering that the headline non-farm payrolls number was only a shade lower than market expectations, traders said.

But the market latched on to the data as an excuse to take profits in the dollar, which had romped to a new 40-month high against the mark earlier, they said. And a U.S. holiday on Friday also encouraged position-squaring by traders there.

The dollar was at 1.7474/84 marks at 1530 GMT, down from its multi-year high of 1.7566 and below the 1.7520/25 seen in late European trade on Wednesday. Dollar/yen was at 113.51/61 against yesterday's 114.38/43.

Regarding the yen, mark/yen was the biggest mover today as it fell through a significant round figure of 65.00. Dollar/yen had been weighed down by mark/yen's weakness and the U.S. jobs data had accelerated the slide, traders said.
June U.S. payrolls rose by 217,000 amid forecasts for an increase of 222,000, while the closely watched average hourly earnings rose by 0.3 percent against expectations of 0.4.

Released the day after the Federal Reserve decided not to raise interest rates at its policy-making meeting, the mild jobs data had dampened expectations of a rate hike in the near future, traders and analysts said.

"The figures were not bad, but the market was counting on quite a strong number and there were many people who were considering selling (dollars) if the data showed anything like a slowdown," said one trader at a Japanese bank in London.
"Then when the data came out the dollar hit some big stops around 114.10-15 yen and the selling came like someone had pulled the plug out," he said.

"We've had the Fed meeting so in a sense it's quite timely that we had some data which, at least in the headline, looks as if the trend in job creation has slowed. It's definitely been a positive factor for both the short and long end of the U.S. yield curve," said Andrew Snowball, treasury economist at Co-operative Bank in London.
But he added that he did not think today's moves signalled a turnaround in the dollar's latest rally.
Meanwhile, some said this week's Fed meeting and today's data had slightly dampened expectations of a rate hike at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting in August.
"The Fed seems content to keep monetary policy steady with the labour market and unemployment at these levels," said Adrian Davies, senior strategist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.
"That tends to suggest that rates won't be raised at the next (FOMC) meeting either, as long as the labour market conditions don't change significantly from what they are now."

Elsewhere, the British pound stormed ahead after the UK budget, unveiled on Wednesday, which the market believed was not stringent enough to curb consumer demand. This led to heightened speculation that the Bank of England would raise interest rates soon to keep the economy under control.
Speculation of a British rate hike in the near term had been swirling in the market for some time and has helped catapult sterling to new multi-year highs every trading day since June 26.
It was trading at its highest in nearly six years at 2.9580/90 marks in late European trade, up from its late Wednesday level of 2.9265/75.
The pound was also strengthening against the dollar, rising to a five-month high of $1.6929. It was at $1.6915/25 in late trade against Wednesday's $1.6700/10.
